hook: Brynjolfsson has spent three decades building the empirical case for how digital technology, and now AI, actually changes productivity and jobs, work that shifted from academic papers to boardroom strategy as generative AI forced every company to ask the same question he had been measuring for years.
name: Erik Brynjolfsson

quote.text: We are entering a period in which our destiny is not to compete with machines, but to figure out how to work with them.
quote.context: A theme repeated across Brynjolfsson's writing and talks, including The Second Machine Age, 2014

moniker: Economist of the Second Machine Age

reading.body:
Brynjolfsson has spent roughly three decades building the empirical case that transformative technologies produce a lag before measurable productivity gains appear, a pattern he formalized as the J-curve and that now frames mainstream debate about generative AI's economic payoff.

His career divides into two recognizable phases. From his 1987 MIT doctorate through the founding of the Stanford Digital Economy Lab in 2019, the work was primarily academic: identifying the productivity paradox of information technology, measuring actual labor-market effects, and resisting both hype and dismissal with data. The Second Machine Age in 2014 and Machine, Platform, Crowd in 2017 carried those findings to a business audience, which is why his framework was already in circulation when generative AI forced every large organization to confront the same questions he had been studying for years.

The co-founding of Workhelix in 2023 marks a deliberate move from measurement to application, translating research on AI's effects on tasks and jobs into consulting for large employers. The data here covers his intellectual development and institutional affiliations; it does not include specific productivity estimates, job-displacement figures, or empirical findings in any detail. It establishes who he is and the arc of his work, not the quantitative content of that work. The J-curve framing is relevant to AI infrastructure investment, since it predicts that compute and building expenditure will precede the productivity gains those investments are supposed to generate, but the data does not connect Brynjolfsson's research directly to power or physical infrastructure constraints.

Co-authored The Second Machine Age (2014) and Machine, Platform, Crowd (2017)
Coined and researched the 'productivity paradox' of information technology
Co-founded Workhelix, applying AI economics research to workforce strategy

achievements.title: Research on the productivity paradox and the 'J-curve' of technology adoption
achievements.impact: Explained why transformative technologies often show a lag before productivity gains appear, a framework now applied directly to generative AI adoption.
